schools.summary: Gill dates the consultation to the gathering that crowned David and, on Lightfoot's authority, puts a long interval before the act, and identifies the congregation as the officers acting for the people.

Henry gives David two aims and three reasons for consulting the leaders, draws from the consultation that no wise prince covets to be absolute, and marks the address to the people as brethren and as a remnant left.

Clarke reports the Targum running the muster from the Nile to the entrance of Antioch; Wesley sets out the same long interval as Gill, with a second assembly called only after the Philistines were twice repulsed.

Ellicott parses David's condition as two independent clauses, glosses the Levites' cities as cities of their pastures, denies that the ark was ever used as an oracle, and places the southern boundary at the modern Wady el Arish; Keil and Delitzsch contrast the political interest of the older account with the chronicler's religious one.

debates.question: What does it mean that they enquired not at the ark in Saul's days?

sides.position: The ark was neglected, the people contenting themselves with sacrificing at Gibeon
Render we sought it not; and perhaps the suffix refers to God rather than the ark, since there is no clear evidence the ark was ever used as an oracle

debates.question: Where was the southern limit of the muster?

sides.position: The Nile of Egypt, with Hemath as the entrance of Antioch, on the Targum's reading
The winter torrent now called Wady el Arish, the same name meaning the Nile only elsewhere

outliers.note: Alone in accounting for the chapter's placement by the compilers' different interests, the older author weighing the transfer politically as an act raising the kingship, the chronicler having in view the restoring of the Levitical worship prescribed in the law.

themes: David consulted with the captains of thousands
if it seem good unto you, and that it be of the Lord
let us bring again the ark of our God
from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath
1.pericope_label: Let us bring again the ark of our God: all Israel from Shihor unto Hemath

schools.summary: Henry draws six lessons from the death of Uzza, refuses to excuse David for stopping the work, and makes the blessing on the house an encouragement to welcome God's ordinances.

Clarke explains the new cart as a precaution against profaning the ark, follows the Targum on the invoking of the Name, and ends with the rabbinical account of the blessing and his own verdict on it; Wesley carries two of Henry's lessons over almost word for word.

Ellicott states the principle governing his notes, that the differences from the older account are abridgments, paraphrases and corrections, and applies it to the place-names, the instruments, the threshing-floor and the obscure phrase about Uzza's hand.

debates.question: How is the clause about the Name to be read?

sides.position: The name was not called upon the ark but invoked at it, with the Targum
The Hebrew as it stands gives who is called Name, a word meaning upon it having dropped out, so that the ark was called by the name of the Lord

debates.question: Was David right to break off the removal?

sides.position: No: he should have gone on notwithstanding the breach, and so it might have been made up, such providences being meant to drive us from our sins and not our duty

outliers.note: Alone in reporting the Targum's account of the blessing, that Obed-edom's wife and his eight daughters-in-law each bore eight at a birth so that fathers and children numbered eighty-one in a day, with the dry verdict that rabbins must be allowed to deal in the marvellous.
